However, the advantage of the Platinum SCM came from achieving comparable performance while requiring a notably smaller BESS design: 0.5 MW/1 h versus the 1 MW/4 h of the Gold SCM. Assuming BESS costs scale at the rates of $350/kW and $400/kWh, this would amount to $1.6 million in DER infrastructure savings (71%) compared with the Gold SCM case, and $3 million in overall infrastructure savings compared with the baseline (57%). These savings do, however, come at the cost of requiring a much more sophisticated controller, accurate fleet management, and facility and solar generation forecasts, which would likely be expensive to acquire in their own rights. However, before a system can be deployed, it is critical that software performance operates cohesively with real-world hardware. In order to stress test the Gold and Platinum management solutions identified above, the team developed a CHIL/power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) test bed to perform real-time control and optimization tests with detailed physics models to represent real- world hardware responses, operating alongside actual EVSE hardware. This emulation/test environment serves as a stress test for the SCM, with full-system control and communication requirements mirroring those of a field demonstration and site deployment. While the controls must manage two EVSE in the lab, hundreds of additional CHIL devices scale up the management and communication requirements to verify at-scale performance. These CHIL end node devices representing individual assets—including DER and EVSE—receive the same control signals as the EVSE and emulate the true physics response as characterized in testing to enable full-scale testing. This setup will mimic the demands of a full rental fleet to de-risk field demonstrations and deployments by verifying performance at scale. 5.1 Lab Demonstration Test Bed 5.1.1 Test Bed Architecture The test bed consists of hundreds of Raspberry Pi 4 Model B devices, each operating as an independent CHIL device to emulate the charging behavior of a specific EV. In a hardware-in- the-loop setup, real hardware components interact with a simulated environment in real time, enabling realistic testing without requiring the complete physical system. Based on experimental hardware test results, a code that models the relationship between the EV state of charge and charging power for different EV and EVSE types was developed and deployed on the CHIL devices.
